scenes.narration: Three hundred and fifty-five billion. That is how many payments carried Visa's name in a single year. Close to one billion every single day.
And yet Visa does not lend you money. Neither does Mastercard. They did not even start as companies. They started as clubs, owned by the banks that used them.
So how did two clubs of banks become the gate that almost every card payment in America has to pass through?
By the end of this video, you will know how that gate was built, why it is so hard to go around it, and why the courts and Congress keep trying to pry it open.

scenes.narration: The story starts in California, in nineteen fifty-eight. Bank of America launches a new kind of card, called BankAmericard. The bank does everything itself. It signs up the shoppers, it signs up the stores, and it carries the risk. It is one bank, running one closed system.

But one bank can only reach so far. So in nineteen sixty-six, according to the Federal Reserve's own history, Bank of America starts licensing the card to other banks, in the United States and abroad. That same year, a group of rival banks forms its own answer, a cooperative called Interbank. In nineteen sixty-nine, it takes the name Master Charge. That is the ancestor of Mastercard.

keyframes.cue: it takes the name Master Charge
keyframes.label: items[3].at.cue

scenes.narration: The BankAmericard system was struggling. In nineteen sixty-nine, a banker named Dee Hock gathered a group of bankers at a hotel in Sausalito to redesign it. The answer was radical. Bank of America would give the system away.

In nineteen seventy, ownership passed to the banks that issued the card. The network became a club, a corporation with no shares for sale, owned by its members. In nineteen seventy-six, after an internal contest, the club chose a new name, one that sounds the same in almost every language. Visa.

keyframes.cue: sounds the same in almost every language
keyframes.label: items[7].at.cue

scenes.narration: Let me draw why the club worked. Before, every bank had its own card, and each card worked only in its own stores. Here is bank A, with its stores. Here is bank B, with its stores. Now put both inside one club. Suddenly every card works in every store of every member. Each bank keeps its own customers, but they all share one network.

keyframes.cue: Now put both inside one club
keyframes.label: strokes[4].start.cue

keyframes.cue: every card works in every store
keyframes.label: strokes[5].start.cue

scenes.narration: For almost forty years, that is what Visa and Mastercard were. Clubs owned by thousands of banks. Then the club turned into a company.

keyframes.label: Clubs owned by thousands of banks…
…then the club turned into a company

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Mastercard went first. In May two thousand six, it sold shares to the public for the first time, at thirty-nine dollars each. The offering raised two point four billion dollars. And most of the money went straight back to the old owners, the banks, to buy back their shares.

Before its own listing, Visa in the United States was owned by about fourteen thousand banks and other financial institutions. In March two thousand eight, in the middle of a financial crisis, Visa went public. It sold four hundred and six million shares at forty-four dollars each. By our calculation, that is about seventeen point nine billion dollars. Visa itself calls it one of the largest stock offerings in history.

Why sell? Part of the reason was the courts. Stores had been suing the card networks for years, saying the banks inside the club were setting fees together. As public companies, Visa and Mastercard would be businesses in their own right, not clubs of competing banks. Merchant lawyers even asked courts to undo the listings.

Let me draw the change. Before, the banks owned the network, and the network served the banks. After, the network is owned by shareholders. The banks become customers. The network is now a business with its own interests, and its own share price.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: And it became a very, very large business. Because of a force that is almost impossible to compete against.

keyframes.label: …and a force that is almost impossible to compete against

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In twenty eighteen, the Supreme Court described what a card network is. It called it a two-sided platform, serving two groups at once, card holders and merchants. And it said these platforms have what economists call indirect network effects. The network is worth more to stores when more shoppers carry its cards, and worth more to shoppers when more stores accept them.

That creates a loop. More cards bring more stores. More stores bring more cards. The Court also noted that almost every bank offering credit cards is in the Visa or Mastercard network, because both began as bank cooperatives.

Look at the size of that loop today. Visa reports five billion payment credentials, more than four hundred million places that accept them, and eighteen trillion dollars in total volume in its latest year. Mastercard reported ten point six trillion dollars in gross volume in twenty twenty-five.

Among the big card networks, the gap is enormous. In Visa's annual report, citing industry data, Visa handled about fourteen point six trillion dollars in payments in twenty twenty-five. Mastercard, about eight point eight trillion dollars. American Express, the next one, about one point nine trillion dollars.

Let me draw the moat. Here is a new network, trying to start. No store will accept it, because nobody carries the card. Nobody will carry the card, because no store accepts it. On the other side, Visa and Mastercard, with billions of cards and hundreds of millions of stores. The loop that made them big is the same loop that keeps others out.

keyframes.cue: The loop that made them big
keyframes.label: actions[0].at.cue

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: But a moat can also be dug deeper on purpose. And that is where the government stepped in.

keyframes.label: A moat can be dug deeper on purpose…

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: By the late nineteen nineties, Visa and Mastercard had rules for their member banks. A bank could issue their cards, but it could not issue American Express or Discover cards. The government sued. According to its brief, Visa and Mastercard then accounted for seventy-three percent of general purpose card transactions, and eighty-five percent of cards issued.

The courts agreed with the government. The rules had worked as intended. No bank in the continental United States had agreed to issue American Express cards. Visa and Mastercard were ordered to repeal them, and in two thousand three, the appeals court upheld that order.

Then Congress went after debit cards. A law passed in twenty ten, known as the Durbin Amendment, told the Federal Reserve to limit debit fees for large banks. Today the cap is twenty-one cents, plus five hundredths of a percent of the purchase, plus one cent for fraud prevention. The law also requires every debit card to work on at least two unrelated networks.

In twenty twenty-three, the Fed proposed lowering that cap. On an average fifty dollar purchase, it would fall from twenty-four and a half cents to seventeen point seven cents. That proposal has still not become final. Meanwhile, two federal courts reached opposite decisions on whether the cap itself is valid, and for now it stays in effect.
Europe went further. Since twenty fifteen, European Union law has capped the fee banks earn on consumer cards at zero point two percent for debit and zero point three percent for credit.

Let me draw the walls of the gate. First, the exclusivity rules, torn down by the courts. Second, the debit cap and the two-network rule, set by Congress. Third, Europe's caps. Each one opened a small door. None of them removed the gate.

keyframes.cue: Each one opened a small door
keyframes.label: strokes[4].start.cue

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: And now the gate itself is on trial.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In September twenty twenty-four, the Justice Department sued Visa. It alleges that Visa illegally protected a monopoly in debit. According to the complaint, more than sixty percent of debit transactions in America run on Visa's network, letting it charge more than seven billion dollars in fees a year. These are allegations. In twenty twenty-five, a judge refused to dismiss the case, and it is still going on.
The complaint even quotes Visa's own description of the network effects around its business. An enormous moat.

The stores have their own case, and it has run for about twenty years. In twenty nineteen, a court approved a settlement for the merchants. By our arithmetic, after money returned for stores that opted out, it came to about five and a half billion dollars. A second deal, in twenty twenty-four, was rejected by the judge.

A new deal was signed in November twenty twenty-five. It would cut the average credit card fee by a tenth of a percentage point for five years. And stores could choose to refuse premium cards, while still accepting standard ones. It won preliminary approval in twenty twenty-six. Final approval is still pending.

And in Congress, a bill called the Credit Card Competition Act was reintroduced in January twenty twenty-six. Banks with more than one hundred billion dollars in assets would have to offer a second network on credit cards, one outside Visa and Mastercard. It has not passed. Visa itself says it is unclear whether the bill will gain enough traction.

Let me draw where the pressure comes from. The Justice Department, on debit. The stores, through the courts. Congress, with a second network for credit. Three forces pushing on the same gate. So far, the gate is still standing.

keyframes.cue: Let me draw where the pressure
keyframes.label: strokes[0].start.cue

scenes.narration: So how did Visa and Mastercard become gatekeepers? Not by lending money, and not by owning stores. They became the meeting point. First as clubs that let thousands of banks act like one. Then as companies sitting on a loop that gets stronger every time someone opens a card or a store accepts one. That is the real business. Not the plastic, but the place where everyone has to meet.
